1.pericope_label: And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, wherein Solomon had built the house of the Lord, and his own house, That the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there. And Solomon went to Hamath–zobah, and prevailed against it. And he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities, which he built in Hamath. Also he built Beth–horon the upper, and Beth–horon the nether, fenced cities, with walls, gates, and bars; And Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and all the chariot cities, and the cities of the horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his dominion.

schools.summary: Ellicott spends his longest note on the Huram cities, sets out three explanations of the contradiction with Kings, adopts the reading that the chronicler passed over the surrender of the territory and spoke of Huram's non-acceptance as a gift, and defends that against the charges of effacement and remodelling; he also identifies Tadmor as Palmyra on the traders' route, reads the store cities as outposts against the neighbouring kingdom, and notes what the chapter leaves out. Delitzsch frames the chapter in four notices before reading it, and presses the verb for completing rather than fortifying.

Gill reports the exchange of cities flatly, and identifies the march on Hamath-zobah as the only instance of any warlike expedition of Solomon's, against Coelesyria, which David had subdued and which had perhaps rebelled.
Clarke does the arithmetic of the twenty years, seven years and a half for the temple and twelve and a half or thirteen for the palace, and identifies Tadmor as Palmyra in a line.

Henry reads the building list for character rather than geography, that Solomon spent his days not in his study but in his country, that a state should promote industry and keep its subjects from idleness, and that he knew how to set bounds to his desires, unlike Alexander fretting for more worlds to conquer.

debates: Why this text has Huram giving cities to Solomon where Kings has Solomon giving cities to Huram: Josephus and the English version make it a return of the despised cities, others an exchange of friendly gifts, which Ellicott calls highly improbable, and Ellicott himself a deliberate silence about the surrender.

Whether the Hamath-zobah expedition was a conquest of the kingdom or, as Ellicott holds with Thenius, only the annexation of part of its territory; the event is recorded nowhere else in the Old Testament.
Whether the verb rendered built means fortified or completed, where Delitzsch argues for completion because the cities were in very bad condition.
outliers: Ellicott defends the chronicler's version as neither an effacement nor a travesty nor a remodelling in Solomon's favour, but another statement equally true and not incompatible with the older one.
Ellicott reports that Solomon's founding of Palmyra is still the tradition of the country.
themes: And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, wherein Solomon had built the house of the Lord, and his own house,
That the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there.
And Solomon went to Hamath–zobah, and prevailed against it.
And he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities, which he built in Hamath.
Also he built Beth–horon the upper, and Beth–horon the nether, fenced cities, with walls, gates, and bars;

And Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and all the chariot cities, and the cities of the horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his dominion.

8.pericope_label: But of their children, who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel consumed not, them did Solomon make to pay tribute until this day. But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants for his work; but they were men of war, and chief of his captains, and captains of his chariots and horsemen. And these were the chief of king Solomon’s officers, even two hundred and fifty, that bare rule over the people. And Solomon brought up the daughter of Pharaoh out of the city of David unto the house that he had built for her: for he said, My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places are holy, whereunto the ark of the Lord hath come.

schools.summary: Delitzsch corrects the list of officers twice, reordering the words to match Kings and insisting that one title means royal adjutants rather than chariot combatants, and resolves the two hundred and fifty overseers against the five hundred and fifty of Kings by nationality rather than emendation; Ellicott places the Egyptian princess in the dynasty founded by Shishak, marks the stated motive as characteristic of this writer, and declines to follow Thenius on where she could have lived.

Clarke takes the removal as evidence in Solomon's favour, that he considered his wife a heathen unfit to dwell in a sanctified place and had not yet departed from the true God, and passes on a later tradition that names her Bithiah; Wesley makes it a precaution, the ark being then in the house of David, which ought to be kept free from the very danger and appearance of pollution.

Henry works the contrast between a house of great piety and a court of perhaps great vanity, doubts that all the princess's servants were proselyted, grants that Solomon lacked the zeal to punish what was amiss, and guards the argument from proving too much before drawing his own principle about the ancient landmarks.

debates: Whether the two hundred and fifty overseers of this text can be reconciled with the five hundred and fifty of Kings, which Delitzsch does by making these Israelites and the larger figure the chief overseers of both nations.

What the removal of Pharaoh's daughter shows about Solomon: evidence that he still held the true God (Clarke), a precaution about the ark (Wesley), or a half-measure by a king who would not punish what was amiss (Henry).
Whether the princess could have lived anywhere but the old palace of David until the new house was finished, as Thenius held and Ellicott denies.
outliers: Henry blocks the inference that every place the ark had rested in became holy, since the houses of Abinadab and Obed-edom would then have been so too.
themes: But of their children, who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel consumed not, them did Solomon make to pay tribute until this day.
But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants for his work; but they were men of war, and chief of his captains, and captains of his chariots and horsemen.
And these were the chief of king Solomon’s officers, even two hundred and fifty, that bare rule over the people.

And Solomon brought up the daughter of Pharaoh out of the city of David unto the house that he had built for her: for he said, My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places are holy, whereunto the ark of the Lord hath come.

12.pericope_label: Then Solomon offered burnt offerings unto the Lord on the altar of the Lord, which he had built before the porch, Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles. And he appointed, according to the order of David his father, the courses of the priests to their service, and the Levites to their charges, to praise and minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required: the porters also by their courses at every gate: for so had David the man of God commanded. And they departed not from the commandment of the king unto the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures. Now all the work of Solomon was prepared unto the day of the foundation of the house of the Lord, and until it was finished. So the house of the Lord was perfected.

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the verbs and the plural form of the set seasons, notes that the altar standing before the porch is absent from Kings, wants the dropped preposition restored on three manuscripts and the versions, and divides the closing verse into two periods while reporting that all the versions take the phrase the other way; Delitzsch reads the daily rate as an explanatory clause interpolated into the main sentence, declines the emendation because the verb takes an accusative in the sense of transgressing, and fixes the day as the one on which regular worship began.

Gill supplies the twenty-four courses serving weekly in their turns, insists the sacrificing was his constant practice and not merely the moment of the rebuilding, reads the commandment as Solomon's own according to the order of David, and takes the preparation to be of materials and expenses.

Clarke identifies the king's commandment as the institutions of David in five words; Wesley reads the man of God as a prophet inspired in these matters whose commands are therefore the commands of God, and the preparation as materials fitted and completed beforehand.

Henry notices that David is given the title Moses bore and for the same reason, draws the lesson from Solomon's refusal to amend or add to what the man of God had commanded, and says what the perfecting consisted in, that the work was the main matter and not the place.

debates: Whose commandment none departed from: the institutions of David (Clarke, Ellicott, Delitzsch) or Solomon's own command issued according to David's order (Gill).
Whether the Hebrew needs mending at verse 15, where Ellicott restores a dropped preposition on manuscript and version authority and Delitzsch holds no alteration necessary.

What was prepared and until when: the materials procured beforehand (Gill, Wesley), the work completed in two periods up to and then from the foundation (Ellicott, who notes the versions read it the other way), or the arrangements finished by the day regular worship began (Delitzsch).
outliers: Ellicott observes that the plural form used here for the set seasons occurs nowhere else.
Henry puts Solomon's authority as a sequence: he observed God's laws, and then all obeyed his orders.
themes: Then Solomon offered burnt offerings unto the Lord on the altar of the Lord, which he had built before the porch,

Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.

And they departed not from the commandment of the king unto the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures.

17.pericope_label: Then went Solomon to Ezion–geber, and to Eloth, at the sea side in the land of Edom. And Huram sent him by the hands of his servants ships, and servants that had knowledge of the sea; and they went with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and took thence four hundred and fifty talents of gold, and brought them to king Solomon.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that the text implies a personal visit, holding that Solomon sent his shipwrights to the port in Edom, collects the variant readings of the place-name and the sea, and works the question of how Tyrian ships reached the gulf as a dilemma that dissolves, concluding that the vessels were left at Joppa while part of their crews went on overland; he also explains the difference in the talents as two Hebrew letters confused. Delitzsch dates the voyage to the second half of the reign and places Ophir in southern Arabia rather than India.
Gill supplies only the occasion, that the king was now at leisure to look after his navy and carry on his merchandise.

Clarke leaves the port and Ophir to conjecture, and divides the enterprise by the character of the two peoples: Solomon probably bore the expenses while the Tyrian king furnished the expert sailors, the Jews having at no period any skill in maritime affairs.

Henry takes the journey literally and makes a maxim of it, that those who deal much in the world should inspect their affairs themselves, then reads the whole enterprise as a lesson in dependence ending in grace rather than gold being the best riches.

debates: Whether Solomon went down to the coast in person, as Henry reads it and makes a maxim of, or sent his shipwrights, as Ellicott holds the words do not necessarily imply.
Where Ophir lay, which Delitzsch places in southern Arabia against the commoner identification with India, and Clarke leaves to conjecture.
How the Tyrian ships reached the gulf: dragged overland across the desert, sailed round Africa, or, as Ellicott concludes, never taken past Joppa at all.
outliers: Ellicott grants that both rejected alternatives are possible, since the Greek historians speak of transporting ships overland and the circumnavigation of Africa was achieved by an expedition sent out by Necho some four centuries later.
themes: Then went Solomon to Ezion–geber, and to Eloth, at the sea side in the land of Edom.

And Huram sent him by the hands of his servants ships, and servants that had knowledge of the sea; and they went with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and took thence four hundred and fifty talents of gold, and brought them to king Solomon.
